## Leviticus 17: Notes

**Overview**
- Matthew Henry says the chapter's two bans (sacrificing away from the tabernacle, and eating blood) exist to protect the honour of the atonement set out in Leviticus 16. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_017.cfm
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary calls the chapter "Holiness in Eating." It says the rules can look ceremonial, but they are all about keeping idolatry out of how food is prepared and eaten. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm

**vv. 1–4: Sacrifice only at the tabernacle**
- Guzik says the Hebrew word for "kill" or "slaughter" in v. 3 is the technical word for sacrificing, not for ordinary butchering. Now that the tabernacle had been built (Exodus 40), Israel had one central place of worship. Sacrifices had to be brought there and offered by the priests. Anyone who refused was "cut off," which Guzik takes to mean exiled from the community. He applies this against modern do-it-yourself spirituality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- Calvin (Reformed) gives two reasons God required one place and one priesthood:
  - Allowing altars everywhere would have corrupted pure worship.
  - It pointed the people to the Mediator, since no offering is acceptable except by His grace.

  He reads "kill" here as limited to sacrifices, because elsewhere the people may eat meat in any town as long as they avoid the blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/17.htm
- **Where readers differ on v. 3:** this is a split between individual commentators, not between denominations.
  - The Expositor's Bible Commentary says every animal fit for sacrifice had to be treated as a peace offering. No private person could slaughter one anywhere except at the tent's entrance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm
  - Matthew Henry records the view that this applied to all slaughter for food in the wilderness. He leans against it, because v. 7 calls the law a "statute for ever." He prefers the reading that it bans sacrificing anywhere but God's altar. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_017.cfm
- Bible.org says most of these offences are labelled "bloodguiltiness." https://bible.org/book/export/html/6234

**vv. 5–6: Bringing field sacrifices to the priest**
- Guzik says an Israelite could not follow his own heart or feelings in worship; he had to come the way God provided. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- Precept Austin cites a comment that Israel picked up sacrificing "in the open field" from the Egyptians, kept falling back into it at groves and high places, and that this was the snare of their whole later history. The page also says vv. 1–9 banned offering animals in the fields as was done in worship of the idol Pan. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_17_commentary
- Bible.org says God did not expose the pagan side of these field sacrifices until He had given the remedy, His own sacrificial system. It calls this an example of progressive revelation. https://bible.org/book/export/html/6234

**v. 7: The "goat demons"**
- Guzik says these were demons worshipped in goat form. He links this to Paul's teaching that sacrificing to idols is sacrificing to demons (1 Cor 10:20–21). He reads "prostituted themselves" as covenant adultery, since Israel was Yahweh's "wife." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- Precept Austin says the Hebrew *sa'ir* refers four times to goat idols or demons, which were seen as one and the same. It quotes G. Campbell Morgan:
  - Israel probably worshipped this false god in Egypt, though we "may not dogmatize."
  - The lasting lesson is that right worship of God makes false worship unnecessary.

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_17_commentary
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary links this to goat worship at Mendes in Lower Egypt, citing Ezekiel 20 on Israel worshipping "the idols of Egypt." It thinks everyday slaughter was often tied to some idolatrous ritual and says the law cut this off at the root. It notes that Luther translated the word "field devils." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm
- Matthew Henry likens Israel's attachment to these demons to adultery against the marriage covenant. He says this is why God calls Himself "a jealous God." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_017.cfm

**vv. 8–9: The rule covers foreigners too**
- Guzik says the command covered resident foreigners as well as Israelites, and that "cut off" means put out of the community. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary gives the Gibeonites as an example of such foreigners and says no idolatry was tolerated in the holy camp. Its lesson is that a holy person avoids even doing lawful things in ways that compromise their witness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm
- Calvin says God did not want foreigners' freedom to defile the sanctuary and spread among the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/17.htm

**v. 10: "I will set My face against"**
- Calvin says God here goes beyond ordering judges to act. He takes the punishment on Himself, so offenders do not escape even if the courts miss them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/17.htm
- Bible.org says God's personal involvement is the most sobering part. It quotes a commentator who doubts "cut off" means a court execution, because many of these sins are secret. The quoted view is that it means early death at God's hand and may hint at judgment in the life to come. https://bible.org/book/export/html/6234
- Guzik says animals in Israel were drained of as much blood as possible, and this later became part of kosher practice (citing Rooker). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/

**v. 11: "The life of the flesh is in the blood"**
- Guzik:
  - Pagans reasoned that because life is in the blood, they should drink it to take that life for themselves. The godly Israelite reasoned that it therefore belongs to God.
  - Quoting Rooker: one life is given for another, the innocent victim's blood for the sinner's. Most Old Testament uses of "blood" mean a violent death, so the focus is blood shed, not blood in the veins.
  - Eating blood would make the means of atonement common.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- Precept Austin:
  - Blood was for atonement, not food, and the principle of atonement is life for life.
  - Forgiveness comes not because sin's penalty is excused but because it is transferred to a sacrifice.
  - The Hebrew word for atonement, *kaphar*, is also used for appeasing anger and for coating wood with pitch, and it expresses God covering sin.
  - Christ's blood means His life given as a substitute.

  https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_17_commentary
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary says the bans on blood and fat reminded Israel at every meal of two things: atonement by blood is the only basis for acceptance, and God has a claim on the redeemed person's best. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm
- Calvin says Moses indirectly rebukes ingratitude. God withheld the blood for the altar, for reconciliation, which was something better than food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/leviticus/17.htm
- Bible.org's application: people who value Christ's blood claim it every time they come to God, not just once. https://bible.org/book/export/html/6234

**v. 12: The ban repeated**
- **A disputed modern view:** Precept Austin says Jehovah's Witnesses use this verse to forbid blood transfusions (*Reasoning from the Scriptures*, 1989). The page answers this from the evangelical side. It also says Jesus' words about drinking His blood (John 6) were not literal but about His work of redemption. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_17_commentary
- I found no Catholic or Orthodox page to set against that reading of John 6.

**vv. 13–14: Blood from hunted animals**
- Guzik says hunted animals could not be bled the normal way, so the blood was poured out and covered with dust. He argues this honoured the blood rather than disrespecting it, comparing Uzzah's mistake of treating the ground as dirtier than his own touch (2 Sam 6:6). He applies it to how we regard Jesus' blood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary says a deer's blood could not be used in sacrifice, but it was still blood, so it had to be treated with respect. It warns against speaking lightly of sacred things. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm
- Matthew Henry says God wanted His people to respect even their animals' lives and not be cruel or bloodthirsty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_017.cfm
- Precept Austin says no one, Israelite or foreigner, could hunt just for sport while ignoring that the blood is sacred. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_17_commentary

**vv. 15–16: Eating an animal found dead or mauled**
- Matthew Henry says these animals were not to be eaten because their blood had not been drained, or not properly. God wanted His people careful about food in a way that restrains appetite rather than indulging it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_017.cfm
- Guzik notes that Deuteronomy 14:21 lets a foreigner eat an animal that died naturally. So he thinks the "foreigner" in vv. 15–16 means converts to Israel's faith, not every outsider. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-17/
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary says that even for game, ceremonial washing was needed before the person could resume his covenant standing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/17.htm
